plan.contextChunk:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from
images is the **aperture problem**. The aperture problem happens when
observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the
image frame, as shown in @fig-apperture_problem. If none of the
termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the
aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the
component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

![Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what is visible within the observation window, appears as if the motion of the bar is in the direction perpendicular to the bar.](figures/optical_flow/apperture_problem.png){width="100%" #fig-apperture_problem}


:::{.column-margin}
The **Barber-pole illusion** is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

![](figures/optical_flow/barber_pole.png){width="40%"}
:::


### Representation of Optical Flow

We can model motion over time as a sequence of **dense optical flow**
images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at
time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation
is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory
followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the
location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a **sparse set of
moving points** (tracks):
$$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This has the challenge

elements: vertical cylinder representing the barber pole
helical stripe pattern mapped onto the cylinder (red, white, blue, white)
top flat ellipse of the cylinder, outlined in black
curved horizontal arrow above the cylinder indicating 'Real motion' (rotation)
vertical arrow to the right of the cylinder indicating 'Observed motion' (downward)
optional circular aperture overlay (a dark semi-transparent mask with a circular cutout) to isolate a single patch of the stripe boundary
local motion vector arrows at the stripe boundary (perpendicular normal component vs. true horizontal motion)

interactions.label: Rotation Speed
interactions.teaches: Reversing or speeding up the rotation directly changes the speed and direction of the perceived vertical movement, demonstrating the illusion's dependency on the helix angle.

interactions.label: Show Local Aperture
interactions.teaches: Places a small circular window over a single stripe boundary. Inside the window, all horizontal cues disappear and only motion perpendicular to the edge is visible.

demo_steps.title: The Barber-Pole Illusion
demo_steps.narration: Watch the cylinder rotate horizontally (Real motion). Because the stripes are helical, our visual system misinterprets this horizontal rotation as a continuous downward sliding motion (Observed motion).

demo_steps.title: Isolating with an Aperture
demo_steps.narration: Activate the aperture window. By masking the top and bottom ends of the pole, we eliminate all boundary 'terminators'. Inside this local aperture, we can only see motion perpendicular to the stripe's edge.

demo_steps.title: Reversing the Real Motion
demo_steps.narration: Reverse the cylinder's rotation. Now, the real motion is in the opposite direction, and the stripes appear to glide upward. This demonstrates how local 1D motion signals are integrated globally to create the illusion of movement.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Front-facing orthographic camera, slightly elevated to look down at the top ellipse of the cylinder, matching the textbook diagram's geometry.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the vertical axis of the cylinder, which runs straight up and down. (2) The cylinder faces the reader directly, meaning the camera is broadside to the rotation axis (azimuth is near 0 or 180 degrees depending on axis setup; we'll use 0 to face the front). (3) The top of the cylinder is visible as an open ellipse rather than a flat line, showing a clear foreshortening cue that implies an elevation of about 15-20 degrees looking downward.

camera_view.view_notes: The cylinder is centered. The elevated camera angle of 18 degrees perfectly captures the top elliptical face of the barber pole, matching the original illustration.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must show the vertical barber pole with its characteristic red/white/blue helical stripes, with the 'Real motion' rotation arrow on top and the vertical 'Observed motion' arrow on the right.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: At most 2 compact controls (rotation speed slider and aperture toggle) placed near the bottom edge without covering the cylinder.
inline_constraints.explainers: Hover tooltips over the arrows should explain the aperture problem physics directly.
inline_constraints.framing: Match the narrow vertical aspect ratio of the original barber pole figure, leaving comfortable margins.
inline_constraints.camera: The initial render must align perfectly with the textbook's visual perspective of the pole.

interactionPlan.notes: The helical stripes can be created in Three.js by mapping a repeating canvas texture containing angled stripes onto a CylinderGeometry. When the rotation speed is non-zero, continuously increment the cylinder's rotation.y. If 'apertureMode' is enabled, render a dark screen-space overlay with a transparent circular stencil mask centered on one of the stripe boundaries.

phase2Evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis:
Core concept: The aperture problem illustrated via the Barber-pole illusion, where horizontal rotation of a helical pattern is perceived as vertical motion because local edge detectors can only measure motion perpendicular to the edge (normal flow). 

User-visible claims and features:
1. 'Real motion' (horizontal rotation) and 'Observed motion' (downward sliding) labels and arrows: Highly accurate representation of the physical cylinder rotation versus the human visual illusion.

4. Educational popups/tooltips: Accurately define the role of 'stripe terminators' at cylinder boundaries in helping resolve ambiguity, and how hiding them produces the aperture problem.
phase2Evaluation.notes: The figure is exceptionally well-implemented, achieving perfect scores in both conceptual accuracy and interactivity. It flawlessly demonstrates the barber-pole illusion and the aperture problem with functional speed controls, an aperture mask toggle, and accurate motion vector indicators.
